what_moved: The headline numbers held flat (KIUC still cites 81% restored on its Sept 14 restatement, death toll still 3, Major Disaster Declaration still not approved), but real day-2 detail layered on top: (1) nearly all Kauai public schools reopened Sept 14, with the two remaining North Shore closures — Hanalei and Kilauea Elementary — now targeted for Sept 15 reopening (this was a total unknown in the Sept 14 baseline); (2) Kauai's harbors came back — Nawiliwili open to cargo (no cruise ships yet) and Port Allen open for operations — a status not previously reported; (3) resident-submitted damage assessments rose from 464+ to 550+; (4) the Hawaii congressional delegation formally escalated by sending a joint letter to Trump on Sept 14 pressing for both the Lowell and Lala major-disaster approvals, citing five disasters in six months; (5) North Shore outage scope got a sharper number — ~5,000 accounts on the North Shore transmission line remain dark, versus the vaguer ~8,400 island-wide figure from Sept 12-13; (6) Kuhio Highway status refined to \"open to local traffic only\" Princeville-to-Ke'e with active debris/lane-shift operations, and the Wainiha double bridge still under the 5-ton local-traffic-only restriction. This is enough new, specific, sourced movement to justify a day-2 follow-up video even though the top-line 81%/pending-declaration/3-deaths figures themselves did not change.
as_of_line: As of Sunday-Monday Sept 13-14, 2026 Hawaii time (Sept 14-15 IST): KIUC restoration holds at 81% (same figure restated Sept 14, +1,850 more customers Sunday), ~5,000 North Shore accounts still out; nearly all Kauai DOE schools reopened Sept 14, Hanalei and Kilauea Elementary targeted for Sept 15; Nawiliwili and Port Allen harbors both back to limited operations; resident damage reports now above 550; Hawaii's congressional delegation formally pressed Trump on Sept 14 for the still-pending Lowell and Lala major disaster declarations; death toll unchanged at 3; Gov. Green's $400M Kauai damage estimate (Sept 9) stands, no FEMA-validated Lowell-specific dollar figure exists yet.

facts.fact: KIUC restored power to 81% of members by Sunday Sept 13/14, with about 1,850 additional customers restored that day; the headline percentage is unchanged from the Sept 13 figure.
Approximately 5,000 accounts served by the North Shore transmission line remain without power as of the Sept 14 update — a sharper, narrower figure than the prior island-wide ~8,400-out estimate.
Scattered pocket outages persist in Anahola, Kapaa, Wailua, Lihue, Poipu, Omao, Kalaheo, Lawai, Hanapepe, Kaumakani, and Kokee.
First North Shore restorations (Kilauea, Princeville, Hanalei) are expected early this week; no full restoration date exists because of extensive damage along Powerline Road.

Nearly 100 mutual-aid personnel from Hawaiian Electric, Southern California Edison, and HMS Construction have arrived; the U.S. Air Force airlifted six SCE utility trucks from California; KIUC has about 250 personnel deployed on restoration.
KIUC suspended collections on delinquent accounts during storm recovery and is urging safety precautions around gas-powered generators.

Hawaii's congressional delegation (Sens. Schatz, Hirono; Reps. Case, Tokuda) sent a formal letter to President Trump on Sept 14 urging approval of both the Hurricane Lowell (Kauai/Maui) and Hurricane Lala (statewide) major-disaster-declaration requests.
As of Sept 14, no Presidential Major Disaster Declaration has been approved for either Hurricane Lowell or Hurricane Lala; both remain pending White House/FEMA action.
The delegation's letter cites five disasters in six months (March Kona Lows, May Kona earthquake, August Lala, August Tropical Storm Moke, September Lowell) as exceeding state/county capacity.
Nearly all of Kauai's Department of Education public schools reopened to students Sept 14, roughly one week after the storm, with limited school bus service.
Hanalei Elementary and Kilauea Elementary — the two North Shore schools kept closed — are targeted by HIDOE to reopen by Sept 15.
facts.source_name: The Garden Island / Hawaii News Now

facts.fact: Kuhio Highway from Princeville to Ke'e Beach is open to local traffic only as of Sept 14, with active tree/debris removal and single-lane shifts near Kalihiwai Bridge and between the Princeville Transfer Station and Kapaka Street (8:30 a.m.-3 p.m. operations).
The Wainiha double bridge on the Haena side remains open to local traffic only with a 5-ton weight limit while repair work continues.
Nawiliwili Harbor is open to cargo ships (no cruise ships currently calling) and Port Allen is open for operations — the first reported harbor status for Kauai in this recovery.
Resident-submitted storm damage assessments have surpassed 550, up from the 464+ reported on Sept 13.
The Lihue Civic Center remains closed through Friday (Sept 18) for storm-related repairs/cleanup.
The Kauai Police Department issued a public warning Sept 14 about disaster-recovery scams targeting storm-affected residents.

On Lanai, Kaumalapau Harbor resumed limited operations Sept 14 after hurricane-damage repairs, though landside work continues before a full reopening (a separate island, cited for statewide harbor-status context).
Friends of Kamalani and Lydgate Park continue weekly volunteer beach cleanups following storm debris, an ongoing community-recovery thread.

Confirmed Hurricane Lowell death toll stands at 3: a 74-year-old man killed by storm surge on Kauai, a 59-year-old man found dead in Wainiha, and a homeless man on Oahu killed by a falling tree — unchanged since the storm passed.

[Background, >72h] Gov. Josh Green estimated on Sept 9 that Kauai's Lowell damage will exceed $400 million, saying it appeared to have caused more damage than Hurricane Iniki in 1992, previously Hawaii's costliest tropical cyclone.
[Background, >72h] Gov. Green issued a state of emergency for the storm on Sept 3, ahead of Lowell's approach.
[Background, >72h] At peak, Lowell knocked out power to over 91% of Kauai County accounts; Oahu separately recorded about 21,000 outages.

[Background] FEMA's validated Joint Preliminary Damage Assessment tied to Hurricane Lala (not Lowell) separately documents $67 million-plus in statewide Public Assistance-eligible damage; no FEMA-validated dollar figure specific to Lowell has been published as of Sept 14.
facts.source_name: Honolulu Star-Advertiser (context carried in Sept 14 reporting)

facts.fact: [Background, >72h] Lihue Airport reopened Sept 8 after the storm passed.

unknowns: Whether/when Trump and FEMA will formally approve the Hurricane Lowell major disaster declaration for Kauai/Maui counties — still an open request as of Sept 14, now with a fresh congressional delegation letter pressing for it.
Whether/when the separate Hurricane Lala statewide major disaster declaration will be approved.

No FEMA-validated Preliminary Damage Assessment dollar total specific to Lowell alone exists yet — only Gov. Green's own $400M+ estimate; Lala's $67M FEMA-validated PA figure is a separate storm/track.
No confirmed final restoration date for the last North Shore KIUC customers (~5,000 accounts) beyond 'transmission by end of next week.'
No official count of insurance claims filed or paid for Lowell damage has been released by Hawaii's Insurance Division (DCCA) or insurers.
No confirmed reopening date for Hanalei/Kilauea Elementary beyond the Sept 15 target, which is itself not yet verified as met.
No update on injury counts (only the 3-death toll is documented); no indication injuries have been separately tallied.
No firm reopening date for North Shore hotels to new arrivals beyond the previously reported 'no earlier than Oct 1' advisory window.
Exact current island-wide total customers still without power (the 81% figure was restated rather than freshly recalculated on Sept 14; only the North Shore-specific ~5,000 figure is new).
